title: Questions
short: jn (or jn jw) asks a yes-no question; question words include zj "who?", jḫ "what?" and tnj "where?".
trouble: Students confuse question jn with jn "by" (the agent). At the head of a sentence, jn asks a question.

blocks.html: A statement becomes a question in Egyptian by putting a word in front of it, or by putting a question word where the answer would go.

jn (or jn jw) at the head of a sentence asks a yes-or-no question: jn jw=k m pr "are you in the house?", jn sḏm.n=k "have you heard?". Question words stand where the answer would be: zj "who? what?", jḫ "what?", ptr "what? who?", tnj "where?": zj pw "who is it?", jw=k tnj "where are you?".

Many languages mark yes-or-no questions with a word at the front (French "est-ce que", Latin "-ne"). Egyptian uses jn. A question word, on the other hand, replaces the missing piece: in jw=k m pr "you are in the house" the place is m pr; in jw=k tnj "where are you?" tnj takes its slot. In zj pw "who is it?", zj takes the place of a noun in a pw sentence (Sentences with pw).

blocks.html: Spellings of the question words vary: zj is also written zy and sy in older books, tnj also tnw, ptr also pty. The answer boxes accept the common variants.

Confusing the question jn with jn "by", which names the doer after a passive or an infinitive (rdjt ḥtp jn nsw "the giving of an offering by the king", Subjects and Objects of the Infinitive). Check where it stands: at the head of a sentence, before a full statement, jn asks a question; after a verb, before the doer, it means "by". A third use, before a noun and a participle, comes in jn and the Cleft Sentence.
